sections.preamble: You are an expert coding assistant operating inside pi, a coding agent harness. You help users by reading files, executing commands, editing code, and writing new files.
sections.tools:
<tools>
- read: Read file contents
- bash: Execute bash commands (ls, grep, find, etc.)
- edit: Make precise file edits with exact text replacement, including multiple disjoint edits in one call
- write: Create or overwrite files

In addition to the tools above, you may have access to other custom tools depending on the project.
</tools>
sections.rules:
<rules>
- Use bash for file operations like ls, rg, find
- Use read to examine files instead of cat or sed.
- You can inspect PI_* environment variables for current model and session details.
- Use edit for precise changes (edits[].oldText must match exactly)
- When changing multiple separate locations in one file, use one edit call with multiple entries in edits[] instead of multiple edit calls
- Each edits[].oldText is matched against the original file, not after earlier edits are applied. Do not emit overlapping or nested edits. Merge nearby changes into one edit.
- Keep edits[].oldText as small as possible while still being unique in the file. Do not pad with large unchanged regions.
- Use write only for new files or complete rewrites.
- Be concise in your responses
- Show file paths clearly when working with files
</rules>
sections.docs:
<docs>
Pi documentation (read only when the user asks about pi itself, its SDK, extensions, themes, skills, or TUI):
- Main documentation: <vol>/homebrew/lib/node_modules/@earendil-works/pi-coding-agent/README.md
- Additional docs: <vol>/homebrew/lib/node_modules/@earendil-works/pi-coding-agent/docs
- Examples: <vol>/homebrew/lib/node_modules/@earendil-works/pi-coding-agent/examples (extensions, custom tools, SDK)
- When reading pi docs or examples, resolve docs/... under Additional docs and examples/... under Examples, not the current working directory
- When asked about: extensions (docs/extensions.md, examples/extensions/), themes (docs/themes.md), skills (docs/skills.md), prompt templates (docs/prompt-templates.md), TUI components (docs/tui.md), keybindings (docs/keybindings.md), SDK integrations (docs/sdk.md), custom providers (docs/custom-provider.md), adding models (docs/models.md), pi packages (docs/packages.md), environment variables (docs/environment-variables.md), MCP servers (docs/mcp.md), codemode scripts and non-LLM models such as classifiers and image models (docs/codemode.md)
- When working on pi topics, read the docs and examples, and follow .md cross-references before implementing
- Always read pi .md files completely and follow links to related docs (e.g., tui.md for TUI API details)
</docs>

toolsAdded.name: read
toolsAdded.description: Read the contents of a file. Supports text files and images (jpg, png, gif, webp, bmp). Images are sent as attachments. For text files, output is truncated to 2000 lines or 50KB (whichever is hit first). Use offset/limit for large files. When you need the full file, continue with offset until complete.

path.description: Path to the file to read (relative or absolute)

offset.description: Line number to start reading from (1-indexed)

limit.description: Maximum number of lines to read

toolsAdded.name: bash
toolsAdded.description: Execute a bash command in the current working directory. Returns stdout and stderr. Output is truncated to last 2000 lines or 50KB (whichever is hit first). If truncated, full output is saved to a temp file. Optionally provide a timeout in seconds.

timeout.description: Timeout in seconds (optional, no default timeout)

toolsAdded.name: edit
toolsAdded.description: Edit a single file using exact text replacement. Every edits[].oldText must match a unique, non-overlapping region of the original file. If two changes affect the same block or nearby lines, merge them into one edit instead of emitting overlapping edits. Do not include large unchanged regions just to connect distant changes.

path.description: Path to the file to edit (relative or absolute)

oldText.description: Exact text for one targeted replacement. It must be unique in the original file and must not overlap with any other edits[].oldText in the same call.

newText.description: Replacement text for this targeted edit.

edits.description: One or more targeted replacements. Each edit is matched against the original file, not incrementally. Do not include overlapping or nested edits. If two changes touch the same block or nearby lines, merge them into one edit instead.

toolsAdded.name: write
toolsAdded.description: Write content to a file. Creates the file if it doesn't exist, overwrites if it does. Automatically creates parent directories.

path.description: Path to the file to write (relative or absolute)

content.description: Content to write to the file

content.text:
Create an animated, non-interactive surfing pelican using html/3js

Build this as an interactive web page in the current directory.
- The entry point is index.html. Put your code in JavaScript ES modules loaded from it
  (`<script type="module" src="main.js">`), and add a short README.md.
- You may use npm packages: `npm install <package>` here, then import them by name
  (`import * as THREE from "three"`). No CDN URLs and no import maps.
- Afterwards the page is packaged into one self-contained index.html with esbuild: every script and
  stylesheet index.html references is bundled with everything it imports. Load assets the page needs
  with `import` (they become data URLs) or generate them in code, never by URL string.
- The packaged page runs offline in a sandboxed iframe: no network requests, and no localStorage,
  cookies or other storage (they throw there).
- Check that it packages: `esbuild main.js --bundle --format=esm --outfile=/dev/null` must succeed.
  Don't build or package the page yourself; that happens afterwards.
- Only create or edit files inside the current directory.
- Finish with a short summary of what you built.

```js
import * as THREE from "three";

export function waveHeight(x, z, t) {
  return (
    0.55 * Math.sin(x * 0.28 + t * 1.05) +
    0.34 * Math.sin(z * 0.21 + t * 0.85 + 1.7) +
    0.22 * Math.sin((x + z) * 0.15 + t * 1.5) +
    0.12 * Math.sin(x * 0.52 - z * 0.3 + t * 1.9)
  );
}

export function waveSlope(x, z, t, e = 0.6) {
  const hx = (waveHeight(x + e, z, t) - waveHeight(x - e, z, t)) / (2 * e);
  const hz = (waveHeight(x, z + e, t) - waveHeight(x, z - e, t)) / (2 * e);
  return { hx, hz };
}

export function createOcean() {
  const geo = new THREE.PlaneGeometry(170, 170, 150, 150);
  geo.rotateX(-Math.PI / 2);
  const mat = new THREE.MeshPhongMaterial({
    color: 0x0d7d99,
    specular: 0xbfeaf5,
    shininess: 70,
    flatShading: true,
  });
  const mesh = new THREE.Mesh(geo, mat);
  mesh.receiveShadow = true;

  function update(t) {
    const pos = geo.attributes.position;
    for (let i = 0; i < pos.count; i++) {
      pos.setY(i, waveHeight(pos.getX(i), pos.getZ(i), t));
    }
    pos.needsUpdate = true;
  }
  return { mesh, update };
}
```

# Surfing Pelican 🦩🏄 (well, pelican)

An animated, non-interactive scene built with Three.js: a pelican riding a surfboard
on a stylized low-poly ocean.

## What you'll see

- A procedurally modeled pelican (body, curved neck, beak with pouch, flapping wings,
  wagging tail, orange legs) standing on a red surfboard with a fin and deck stripe.
- A CPU-displaced wave field — the board bobs, pitches, and rolls to follow the local
  wave slope, and the pelican shifts its wings for balance.
- Foam ring, wake, and spray droplets around the board.
- Gradient sky dome, sun with canvas-generated glow, drifting clouds, a palm island,
  warm directional light with soft shadows, and distance fog.

The camera slowly sways on its own — there are no controls; the scene just plays.

## Files

- `index.html` — entry point (loads `main.js` as an ES module)
- `main.js` — renderer, scene, lights, camera, animation loop
- `ocean.js` — wave function, slope, animated ocean mesh
- `rider.js` — surfboard + pelican + foam, with its own animation update
- `sky.js` — sky dome, sun/glow, clouds, palm island

## Notes

- Three.js is installed from npm and imported by name; no CDN, no import maps.
- All assets are generated in code (geometry + a canvas-generated glow texture), so the
  page bundles into a single self-contained `index.html` via esbuild and runs fully offline.

## What I built

An animated, non-interactive **surfing pelican** scene in Three.js:

**Files**
- `index.html` — entry point, loads `main.js` as an ES module
- `main.js` — renderer, scene, fog, lights (warm sun + hemisphere), soft shadows, animation loop, slow cinematic camera sway (no controls)
- `ocean.js` — wave field (sum of traveling sines) + CPU-displaced, flat-shaded low-poly ocean
- `rider.js` — surfboard + pelican + foam, encapsulated with its own `update(t)`
- `sky.js` — gradient sky dome (custom shader), sun with canvas-generated glow sprite, drifting clouds, palm island
- `README.md` — short overview

**Scene highlights**
- **Pelican** built procedurally: ellipsoid body, curved neck, long beak with pouch, eyes with glints, swept-back wings with darker tips, wagging tail, orange legs and feet
- **Wave riding**: the board/pelican group samples the wave height and gradient each frame to bob, pitch, and roll realistically; wings make idle flaps plus occasional big balance flaps, head looks around, spray droplets and a pulsing foam ring/wake trail the board
- **Atmosphere**: red board with fin and deck stripe, sun-matched directional light casting soft shadows on the water, distance fog blending into the horizon, slowly drifting clouds and a palm island in the background

Verified with: `esbuild main.js --bundle --format=esm --outfile=/dev/null` ✓
